# Mobile store distribution

You are helping ship a mobile app on the Apple App Store and Google Play. This skill is about distribution constraints: download size, startup time, offline use, on-device scanning, consumable purchases, and the permission and privacy disclosures the stores require. It does not author requirements and it does not replace the platform or developer plugins.

The guidance is generic. The worked example, used only to make the rules concrete, is a **price-tag scanner**: the shopper points the camera at a shelf tag, the phone reads the prices printed on that tag, and the app keeps a running tally for a shopping trip. A paid download can include a starter set of trip credits. Further packs of credits are consumable in-app purchases. Scanning and the tally work with no network. Buying credits and recovering unused credits need a connection and a backend you run.

## Before you answer

1. Load only the reference file the question needs.
2. Separate three kinds of number, and label which kind you are using:
   - a **store limit** (an upload fails, or install is refused),
   - a **store warning** (the upload succeeds; the store tells the developer or the user the app is large),
   - a **budget** you recommend for this app (tighter than the store limit).
3. Cite the official page for every store number. If a page and this skill disagree, the page wins. Say so.
4. Never print a signing key, a shared secret, a purchase token, an API credential, or the contents of a `.p8` or keystore.

## Reference files

- `references/size-limits.md` — Apple and Google download limits, thinning, On-Demand Resources, app bundles, asset delivery, and why 200 MB is not the hard cap
- `references/budgets.md` — how to set and measure size and startup budgets, including the worked-example numbers
- `references/offline-and-scanning.md` — offline-first behavior, on-device text recognition, and the camera
- `references/purchases.md` — consumable credits, proving a paid download, refunds, and restoring a balance
- `references/privacy-and-permissions.md` — camera and location wording, nutrition labels, privacy manifests, Data safety, and the 2027 location button

## Rules that always apply

- Target a download **well under 100 MB** on each store. The store hard limits are much higher. A small utility should also stay under the warning thresholds.
- The core task must finish with the radio off. Network work (a purchase, a restore, a model download) waits, and the app offers a manual fallback.
- Credits bought with in-app purchase must not expire. Neither store restores a consumable balance. You keep that ledger.
- Do not charge for the camera or for location. Charge for the credits, or for whatever digital good the app actually sells.
- If the person denies the camera or location, the core task still has a path (a typed price, a typed place).
- Do not start a new app on On-Demand Resources or on APK expansion files (OBB).

## Worked-example budgets

Use these when the app is the price-tag scanner, or another app of that size. They are budgets, not store limits. Measure them as `references/budgets.md` describes.

| Budget | Value |
| --- | --- |
| iOS thinned download | ≤ 30 MB |
| Android compressed download | ≤ 25 MB |
| Cold start on a mid-range phone | under 2 seconds, and outside the Android vitals "slow" band |

# Size and startup budgets

Read this when you need a number to aim at, or a way to measure the binary and the launch. Store caps are in `size-limits.md`. A budget is tighter than a cap, and you write it down before the binary grows.

## Set the budget

1. Write two download budgets, one per store, in compressed or thinned download size. Also write an install-size budget if disk use matters.
2. Write startup budgets for cold, warm, and hot start. Say which device class they apply to (a mid-range phone several years old, not the newest flagship).
3. A budget is a fail in your own check, not a store rejection. Say that when you report a measurement.
4. Leave headroom. Apple’s processed size can be larger than the IPA you uploaded, because of DRM and recompression. Play’s `bundletool` estimate is not identical to Play Console.

For a small utility, target **well under 100 MB** on both stores. That keeps you under the 200 MB warning on each store (`size-limits.md`) with room for one or two dependencies.

### Worked example: the price-tag scanner

| Budget | Value | Why this number |
| --- | --- | --- |
| iOS thinned download | ≤ 30 MB | A native or thin client plus Apple’s built-in text recognizer, which adds no model. |
| Android compressed download | ≤ 25 MB | The same app plus a bundled Latin text model, about 4 MB per CPU architecture (`offline-and-scanning.md`). |
| Cold start, mid-range phone | under 2 seconds | Inside the Android vitals “slow” line, with margin. |
| Warm start | under 1 second | The vitals “slow” line is 2 seconds. |
| Hot start | under 0.5 seconds | The vitals “slow” line is 1 second. |

These are example budgets for this kind of app. Raise them only for a feature the app cannot ship without, and record what you refused to add. Do not raise them to make room for a second copy of a recognizer, an unused cross-platform runtime, or an asset pack on the first screen.

Apple does not publish a startup number on the pages this skill uses. Do not invent one and attribute it to Apple. The cold-start budget above is ours. The vitals lines below are Google’s.

## Measure download size

### iOS

Do not treat the `.app`, the `.xcarchive`, or the IPA you upload as the size a person downloads. Those bundles contain files the App Store does not ship, including dSYMs. Source: [Reducing your app’s size](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/xcode/reducing-your-app-s-size).

During development, export an Ad Hoc, Development, or Enterprise archive with app thinning set to all compatible device variants. The export folder contains `App Thinning Size Report.txt`. Compressed size in that report is the download. Uncompressed size is the install. The same page shows how to produce the report from `xcodebuild -exportArchive` with a `thinning` key.

After upload, the accurate numbers are in App Store Connect: TestFlight, the build, Build Metadata, App File Sizes. Read **download size** and **install size** per device variant. A yellow warning means a variant crossed the 200 MB over-the-air download limit. TestFlight builds are larger than the App Store build. The approved binary can still grow slightly. Source: [View builds and metadata](https://developer.apple.com/help/app-store-connect/manage-builds/view-builds-and-metadata/) and the reducing-size page.

Compare the variant for a current phone with the iOS budget. The universal variant is not the number a current phone downloads.

### Android

Play Console computes compressed download size when you upload. Before upload, `bundletool` is the estimate, and it is not identical. Source: [Play app size limits](https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/9859372?hl=en).

After a production release, read Monitor and improve > Android vitals > App size. That page shows download size on a reference device (`XXXHDPI ARMv8`, or the closest configuration you support) and the range across configurations. The same page breaks the size into code/DEX, resources, assets, native libraries, and other, for the last few releases.

To see what Play generated from a bundle, open Test and release > Latest releases and bundles > All app versions > App bundle explorer, then the Delivery tab. The Modules table includes the base module and its download size. Asset packs appear when you have them. The help article that describes this path is [Inspect app versions on the Latest releases and bundles page](https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/9844279?hl=en). On 26 November 2026 a request for that article returned HTTP 404 while still serving a page with that title. If the link fails, use the console path above. [Build and test your Android App Bundle](https://developer.android.com/guide/app-bundle/test) is the developer page for inspecting generated APKs.

Compare the reference-device download with the Android budget, and check the top of the range so one ABI or density does not blow the budget alone. Bundled native code is per architecture. A fat APK is not what Play serves from a bundle. Measure the split the device gets.

## Measure startup

### Android

[App startup time](https://developer.android.com/topic/performance/vitals/launch-time) defines the three starts. A cold start creates the process. A warm start redoes some of that work. A hot start brings an activity that is still in memory to the foreground. Optimize for cold start. Time to initial display is the time until the first frame, including a splash screen. Call `reportFullyDrawn` when the app is actually usable, or a splash will hide a slow start.

Play records this in Android vitals and flags a session as slow at:

| Start | Slow at |
| --- | --- |
| Cold | 5 seconds or more |
| Warm | 2 seconds or more |
| Hot | 1 second or more |

Source: [Android vitals](https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/9844486?hl=en), section “Start-up and loading times”. Vitals records the day’s maximum when the app starts more than once from the same state, and only when a person launches an activity.

Treat those lines as the store’s bad-behavior marks, not as a target. The worked-example budgets sit under them. A 5 second cold start is already a slow session.

### iOS

Read launch metrics from shipping builds in Xcode Organizer ([Analyzing the performance of your shipping app](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/xcode/analyzing-the-performance-of-your-shipping-app)) and from [MetricKit](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/metrickit). The Apple pages this skill uses do not publish a numeric “slow launch” threshold. Report the measurement and the budget. Do not cite a fake Apple limit.

## When a measurement misses the budget

Say what the number was, which variant or device, and which budget it missed. Name the largest slice from the Play breakdown or the thinning report. Cut that slice, or move it off the install path using the rules in `size-limits.md`, before you raise the budget. Do not “fix” a miss by switching the recognizer to a download the first launch depends on. That breaks `offline-and-scanning.md`.

# Offline use and on-device scanning

Read this when the app must work without a network, or when it reads text from the camera. The price-tag scanner is the example. The same split applies to any app whose main task happens somewhere the network is poor.

## Offline-first

The core flow does not wait on the network. For the scanner that flow is: open the camera or accept a typed price, read the tag, choose the price, add the line, show the trip total, and keep the trip if the app is killed.

Put that state in local storage on the device (a database or files in the app’s own storage). The credit balance the UI shows is a cache of the ledger, not a request. Buying a pack, proving the paid download, and recovering credits after a reinstall are the calls that need a network. Queue them and run them when a connection exists. Do not block the open trip on that queue.

If a download can be deleted or can fail, the core flow must not need it.

- Apple On-Demand Resources are deprecated for new apps (`size-limits.md`). Do not put the recognizer there.
- Google Play fast-follow and on-demand asset packs may be removed, and the app must not assume they exist ([Play Asset Delivery](https://developer.android.com/guide/playcore/asset-delivery)). Install-time content is the only Play-delivered content that is present at first launch.
- An unbundled ML Kit model downloads through Google Play services the first time it is used, unless you declare an install-time download. Either way, the first scan can fail with no signal. See below.

A cloud recognizer is a fallback for a photo the on-device model cannot read, and only while online. It is not the primary reader. Sending the photo off the device is also a privacy disclosure (`privacy-and-permissions.md`). The default for the scanner is that the tag image stays on the phone.

Manual entry is part of the core flow, not an error state. The person can type the price when the camera is denied, the model is missing, or the tag is unreadable.

## Text recognition

Pick one on-device recognizer per platform. Do not ship two for the same script.

| Option | Where it runs | Added download | Works offline from install | Use when |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Apple Vision text recognition | On device, in the OS | 0 MB | Yes | iOS. This is the default for the scanner. |
| ML Kit text recognition v2, bundled | On device, linked into the app | About 4 MB per script per CPU architecture | Yes | Android, when the first scan must work with no network. |
| ML Kit text recognition v2, unbundled | On device, model from Play services | About 260 KB per script architecture, then a model download | Not until the model has downloaded | Android, only if you can tolerate a first-run download and you still have a typed-price fallback. |

Sources: [Recognizing text in images](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/vision/recognizing-text-in-images) and [ML Kit text recognition v2 on Android](https://developers.google.com/ml-kit/vision/text-recognition/v2/android). The ML Kit page states the size and the install difference in its comparison table. Bundled Latin is `com.google.mlkit:text-recognition`. Unbundled Latin is `com.google.android.gms:play-services-mlkit-text-recognition`. Read that page for the current artifact versions. Do not copy a version out of this skill into a build file without checking the page.

On iOS, call Vision (`VNRecognizeTextRequest`) on a still frame or a sample buffer. Do not add ML Kit on iOS for the same job. The Apple API is already on the device.

On Android, for the scanner, bundle the scripts you actually read. Latin is the usual shelf-tag script in many markets. Each extra bundled script costs about another 4 MB per architecture, so an unnecessary script is a budget failure (`budgets.md`). If you use the unbundled library, declare the install-time model download in the manifest (`com.google.mlkit.vision.DEPENDENCIES`) or request it through Play services, and still let the person type the price when the model is not there yet. The ML Kit page says requests made before the download finishes produce no results.

Recognition quality depends on pixels on the character, focus, and how much of the frame the tag fills. The ML Kit page asks for at least about 16×16 pixels per character and says there is little gain past about 24×24. For a live scanner, drop frames while a recognition is in flight. CameraX’s default `ImageAnalysis` backpressure (`STRATEGY_KEEP_ONLY_LATEST`) does that. Close the `ImageProxy` when the task finishes.

The scanner reads prices on the one tag in front of the camera. It does not need a catalog, a network price API, or a model of every product.

## Camera

### iOS

Use AVFoundation when you need your own capture pipeline (session, device, photo or video output) and Vision on the frames. [AVFoundation](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/avfoundation) is the capture stack.

Use VisionKit when a system scanning UI is enough. [Scanning data with the camera](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/visionkit/scanning-data-with-the-camera) covers `DataScannerViewController`: live video, highlighting, and text and codes. Check `isSupported` (A12 and later) and `isAvailable` (camera permission and no other restriction) before presenting it. [DataScannerViewController](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/visionkit/datascannerviewcontroller) is the class reference.

`NSCameraUsageDescription` is required for either path. Wording is in `privacy-and-permissions.md`. If the key is missing, the camera API fails at runtime.

Guideline 2.5.14: the person gives explicit consent, and the app shows a clear indication when the camera is recording. Guideline 4.10: you may not charge for the camera itself. The pack of trip credits buys tallies, not camera access. Source: [App Review Guidelines](https://developer.apple.com/app-store/review/guidelines/) (last updated 16 October 2026 on the page read for this skill).

### Android

Use [CameraX](https://developer.android.com/media/camera/camerax) (`ImageAnalysis`) and pass `ImageProxy` frames to ML Kit. Request the camera permission in context, at the moment the person starts a scan, not on a cold launch that is only showing a home screen. Runtime permissions are in `privacy-and-permissions.md`.

If the person denies the camera, both platforms stay usable: the tally accepts a typed price. Do not loop the permission prompt. Do not disable the rest of the app.

# Source: references/privacy-and-permissions.md

# Privacy and permissions

Read this when the app uses the camera or location, or when you are filling in the store privacy forms. The price-tag scanner uses the camera to read a tag. It uses location only if a feature needs it (for example a local tax rate). Both have to be optional for the core tally: a typed price and a typed place still work.

Never print a credential, a device check token, or a purchase token while you are testing these flows.

## Camera wording

### Apple

[`NSCameraUsageDescription`](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/bundleresources/information-property-list/nscamerausagedescription) is required if the app uses a camera API. The system shows your string in the permission dialog. Missing key: the camera API fails at runtime. [Scanning data with the camera](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/visionkit/scanning-data-with-the-camera) walks through adding the key and says the dialog includes the app name and your reason.

Guideline 5.1.1(ii): purpose strings clearly and completely describe the use, and paid functionality must not depend on granting access to the data. Guideline 5.1.1(iv): respect a denial, and offer an alternative where you can. Guideline 2.5.14: explicit consent, and a clear indication while the camera is recording. Source: [App Review Guidelines](https://developer.apple.com/app-store/review/guidelines/).

Write the reason as what the person gets, not as the framework name. For the scanner: “The camera reads the price printed on the shelf tag. The picture stays on this phone.” Do not say “for OCR” or “to improve your experience.” If a later version uploads a failed tag, change the string and the privacy label first. The string and the behavior have to match.

### Android

Request `CAMERA` at runtime, in context, when the person starts a scan. [Request app permissions](https://developer.android.com/training/permissions/requesting) is the runtime-permission guide. Declare `android.permission.CAMERA` in the manifest. If they deny it, open typed entry. Do not send them to settings on the first denial.

[Permissions policy](https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/16909972?hl=en) (the page is titled as a preview of upcoming changes and also contains the current policy): request sensitive permissions in context, only for a feature the listing promotes, and provide an alternative when the person declines. The camera is a restricted permission. Use it for scanning tags, not for anything the listing does not describe.

## Location

Ask only if a feature needs it, and ask at the moment that feature runs, not at launch.

Apple: [`NSLocationWhenInUseUsageDescription`](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/bundleresources/information-property-list/nslocationwheninuseusagedescription). Prefer When In Use. Guideline 5.1.5: location only when it is relevant to a feature, and explain why. Guideline 5.1.1(iv) uses this example: if the person declines location, let them type an address. For a tax rate, that alternative is a typed postal code. [Requesting authorization to use location services](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/corelocation/requesting-authorization-to-use-location-services) is the API page.

Google: foreground location is `ACCESS_COARSE_LOCATION`, `ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION`, or both. Coarse is an area of about 3 square kilometers. Precise is on the order of 50 meters or better. Request the coarser one that still does the job. A postal code usually does not need precise location. Source: [Request location permissions](https://developer.android.com/develop/sensors-and-location/location/permissions).

### Location button from 27 January 2027

Two official texts, both checked on 26 November 2026:

- The developer guide says: if the app targets Android 17 (API 37) or later and only contains features that need location for one session, Play policy requires the location button. Source: [Request location permissions](https://developer.android.com/develop/sensors-and-location/location/permissions), “One-time access”.
- The Play policy page is explicitly a **policy preview**. Its opening summary says, effective **January 27, 2027**: apps targeting Android 17 (API 37+) must use the Android location button for one-time or infrequent location requests, and using `ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION` requires a Play Console declaration of why coarse location or the location button is not enough. The same page’s location section says that, for apps targeting SDK 37, precise location for a one-time user-initiated action must use the location button and declare `onlyForLocationButton`, and that you may request `ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION` only when neither the location button nor coarse location can support the feature. The page says the full policy wins if a summary conflicts with it. Source: [Preview: Permissions and APIs that Access Sensitive Information](https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/16909972?hl=en).

For the scanner, a tax-rate lookup is one-off. Plan on the location button when you target Android 17, prefer coarse location, and keep typed postal-code entry. Do not request background location for this.

## What counts as collection

Data that never leaves the phone is treated differently from data you send to a server. The tag image, the on-device recognition, and a location used only to pick a rate on the phone are in the first group if you do not upload them.

Apple privacy nutrition labels: “Data that is processed only on device is not ‘collected’ and does not need to be disclosed.” If you derive something and send that off the device, judge the derived data on its own. Payment card data entered in Apple’s sheet, which you never receive, is not collected. Source: [App privacy details](https://developer.apple.com/app-store/app-privacy-details/). You still submit the label. Every app needs a privacy policy link in App Store Connect and inside the app (guideline 5.1.1(i)).

Google Play Data safety: the form is required even when you collect nothing, and it needs a privacy policy link. “User data accessed by your app that is only processed locally on the user’s device and not sent off device does not need to be disclosed.” Pseudonymous data that can be re-associated with a person must be disclosed. Ephemeral processing that does leave the device has its own definition on that page. You are responsible for the answers. Source: [Data safety](https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/10787469?hl=en).

A credit-recovery backend that stores an `appTransactionID` or a Play account key is collection if it leaves the device. Declare it. Do not describe that identifier as “no data collected.”

## Apple privacy manifest

Ship a `PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy` in the app, and expect one inside each third-party SDK that collects data or uses a required-reason API. The manifest lists collected data types and the required-reason APIs. Source: [Privacy manifest files](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/bundleresources/privacy-manifest-files).

Required-reason APIs are APIs that can fingerprint a device. [Describing use of required reason API](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/bundleresources/describing-use-of-required-reason-api) says App Store Connect does not accept an app that uses those APIs without a declared reason, starting 1 May 2024. The reason has to match the real use. A third-party SDK declares its own reasons. You cannot cover the SDK’s use from the app manifest. Check plugins and analytics SDKs before you upload. A scanner that only uses the camera, Vision, and local storage may still pull a required-reason API in through a dependency. Look at the privacy report Xcode generates. Do not paste a reason code you have not matched to the API list on that page.

## Accounts

Guideline 5.1.1(v): if the app has no significant account features, it works without a login. If the app supports creating an account, it offers account deletion inside the app. Do not require personal information unless it is core to the app or required by law.

The scanner does not need a name or an email to scan a tag. Prefer `appTransactionID` on iOS over an account (`purchases.md`). If you do create an account on Android because Play does not give you an equivalent id, deletion has to exist in the app, and the Data safety form has to match what you store. The Play help URL `answer/13327111` (account deletion), cited in older notes, returned HTTP 404 on 26 November 2026. Read the current Play policy in Console before you rely on a specific deletion URL.

## Price-tag scanner, minimum disclosures

| Data | Leaves the phone? | Label |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Camera frames used for on-device recognition, then discarded | No | Not collected, on both stores, while this stays true |
| Trip lines and totals stored only on device | No | Not collected |
| Credit ledger on your server, keyed by a store id | Yes | Declare it |
| Precise or coarse location sent to a server | Yes | Declare it. Prefer keeping the lookup on device. |
| Card data entered in the store’s payment sheet | You never receive it | Not collected by you |

Say this in the purpose strings and in the forms. If the implementation changes, change the forms in the same release.

# Purchases, credits, and refunds

Read this when the app sells a digital good, especially a consumable the person can buy again. The worked example is trip credits for the price-tag scanner: the paid download may include a starter set, and further packs are consumable in-app purchases.

A paid download and an in-app purchase are different products. Do not implement the starter credits as a consumable the app buys from itself at install.

## Which store API

Digital goods inside the app go through the store.

- Apple: [StoreKit](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/storekit). Use StoreKit 2. Guideline 3.1.1: unlocking functionality uses in-app purchase. Source: [App Review Guidelines](https://developer.apple.com/app-store/review/guidelines/).
- Google Play: [Google Play Billing](https://developer.android.com/google/play/billing) and [Integrate the Google Play Billing Library](https://developer.android.com/google/play/billing/integrate). [Payments policy](https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/10281818?hl=en): Play’s billing system is required for in-app digital goods (virtual currencies, extra playtime, additional features) unless that policy permits something else. The policy documents alternative billing in some regions. Read it before you add a second checkout. The older help URL `answer/9858738` returned HTTP 404 on 26 November 2026. Do not cite it.

Guideline 2.3.2: the description, screenshots, and previews must show which items need an extra purchase. For the scanner, the listing says the download includes the starter credits and that further packs are bought in the app.

Do not charge for the camera or another built-in capability (Apple guideline 4.10). The product is the credits.

## Consumable credits

A pack of trip credits is a consumable: the person can buy it, use it, and buy it again.

Apple guideline 3.1.1: “Any credits or in-game currencies purchased via in-app purchase may not expire,” and restorable purchases need a restore mechanism. Do not put an expiry date on a credit. Do not delete unused credits because a trip ended or a month passed.

Consumables do not appear in [`Transaction.currentEntitlements`](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/storekit/transaction/currententitlements). That sequence is non-consumables, active subscriptions, and non-renewing subscriptions. Apple will not hand the remaining credit balance back. Unfinished consumables are on `Transaction.unfinished` and `Transaction.all`. Finish the transaction only after the credits are durably granted.

On Play, a consumable is a one-time product you consume after granting it, so it can be bought again. If your app has a backend, consume with `Purchases.products:consume` after you have checked `consumptionState`. A client-only app uses `consumeAsync`. Consuming acknowledges the purchase. Source: the integrate guide linked above.

### Grant, then acknowledge, within three days

Play refunds a purchase you do not acknowledge. The integrate guide says to acknowledge within three days of the purchase, or Play refunds it and revokes the entitlement. The three-day window starts when the state becomes `PURCHASED`, not while it is `PENDING`. Do not acknowledge a pending purchase.

Order of operations:

1. The store reports a purchase (`PURCHASED` / a verified StoreKit transaction).
2. Your backend verifies it with the store (Play Developer API `Purchases.products:get`, or Apple’s signed transaction). Reject duplicates. On Play, `purchaseToken` is the unique key. Do not use `orderId` as the primary key. Promo-code purchases may have no `orderId`. Source: [Fight fraud and abuse](https://developer.android.com/google/play/billing/security).
3. Add the credits to your ledger once.
4. Then acknowledge or consume. On Apple, finish the transaction.

The Billing Library version shown on the integrate page when this skill was written was 9.1.0. Read that page for the version to depend on. Do not freeze this sentence into a build file.

## Proving the download was paid

The starter credits come with the paid app, so you need proof of the app purchase, separate from a pack purchase.

### Apple

[`AppTransaction`](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/storekit/apptransaction) is the signed app purchase. It requires iOS 16, iPadOS 16, or the matching later OS on other platforms. [`appTransactionID`](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/storekit/apptransaction/apptransactionid) is a single id per Apple Account for that app. It stays the same if the person redownloads on any device, gets a refund and buys again, or changes storefront. It exists even when there are no in-app purchases. With Family Sharing, each family member has their own id.

Use `appTransactionID` as the account key for the starter credits if you are not asking the person to create an account. Check `revocationDate` before you treat the purchase as still valid. A reinstall of a paid app is free. Without a ledger of how many starter credits were used, a reinstall looks like a new grant. Record the grant against `appTransactionID` on your backend the first time you see that id.

### Google Play

[Play Integrity verdicts](https://developer.android.com/google/play/integrity/verdicts) expose `accountDetails.appLicensingVerdict` for the account signed in on the device: `LICENSED`, `UNLICENSED`, or `UNEVALUATED`. `LICENSED` means that account installed or bought the app from Play. It is not a stable per-person purchase id. The verdict page notes that on some older devices the account can stay licensed after uninstall. `UNEVALUATED` means Play did not assess licensing (untrusted device, unknown app version, or not signed in).

The older [Licensing Verification Library](https://developer.android.com/google/play/licensing) also answers whether the user is licensed. It does not give you an id equivalent to `appTransactionID`.

So a paid Android app can tell you “this Play account is licensed” and cannot, from the pages above, give you a durable id that survives reinstall without your own record. If you need to grant starter credits once, you need a backend key you choose, and you have to be honest about what identifying data that key is. Creating an account, including a silent guest account, has store consequences in `privacy-and-permissions.md`.

### Paid and free are not symmetric on Play

[Set up your app’s prices](https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/6334373?hl=en): you can change a paid app to free. Once the app has been offered for free, it cannot be changed to paid. Charging later means a new app with a new package name. Decide the paid download before the first production release if you might want it later.

## Restoring credits

Neither store restores a consumable balance.

- Apple’s restore mechanism is for restorable products (non-consumables and subscriptions), which is what guideline 3.1.1’s “restore mechanism” refers to. Consumables are absent from `currentEntitlements`.
- Play will deliver an unconsumed purchase again through `queryPurchasesAsync` until you consume it. After a successful consume, the remaining credit count lives only in your ledger.

Recovering unused trip credits after a reinstall or a new phone is your backend: the Apple `appTransactionID`, or whatever Android key you established, maps to a balance. The phone caches that balance for offline use and reconciles when it is online. A lost phone with tallies that were never synced can overspend. Say that plainly when you design the cache. Do not pretend StoreKit or Play Billing will reconstruct the balance.

## Refunds and revocations

Your own “no refunds” copy does not stop the store. Apple and Google can refund a paid app or a pack. Reconcile the ledger when they do.

- Apple: `revocationDate` on `AppTransaction` for the app purchase, and revocation on the in-app transaction. [App Store Server Notifications](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/appstoreservernotifications) deliver the refund and revoke events to your server. Do not rely on the phone being online to learn about a refund.
- Google: [Voided Purchases API](https://developers.google.com/android-publisher/voided-purchases). [Fight fraud and abuse](https://developer.android.com/google/play/billing/security) says a voided purchase includes cancellations, chargebacks, and developer refunds that revoke, and that unacknowledged purchases which Play auto-cancels are in that set. Claw back credits that were not used. If they were already used, the same page’s example is to allow a negative balance and to limit further purchases until it is positive. Pick one policy and apply it the same way on both stores. Do not leave the person in an active trip with a silent negative balance and no explanation.

Verify on a server before you grant. A client that only trusts a local flag will grant the starter credits again after a reinstall, and will keep credits after a refund.

# Source: references/size-limits.md

# Download size limits

Read this when the question is how large the binary may be, what happens above 200 MB, or whether expansion files or On-Demand Resources are still the way to ship extra bytes.

Label every number as a store limit, a store warning, or a budget. Budgets are in `budgets.md`. The recommendation for a normal app, including the price-tag scanner, is a download **well under 100 MB**. That is a budget. It is not a store cap.

Pages below were re-read on 26 November 2026. If a page has changed, the page wins.

## Apple

Two different limits are easy to mix up. The 4 GB figure is the maximum **uncompressed app size**. The 200 MB figure is the **over-the-air download** threshold App Store Connect warns on. 4 GB is not the cellular download cap.

| What | Number | Kind | Source |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Maximum uncompressed app size, iOS 9 and later | 4 GB | Store limit | [Maximum build file sizes](https://developer.apple.com/help/app-store-connect/reference/app-uploads/maximum-build-file-sizes/) |
| Maximum executable size (`__TEXT` sections, total), iOS 9 and later | 500 MB | Store limit | same page |
| Any device variant whose download size exceeds this | 200 MB | Store warning, called the over-the-air download limit | [View builds and metadata](https://developer.apple.com/help/app-store-connect/manage-builds/view-builds-and-metadata/) |

[Reducing your app’s size](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/xcode/reducing-your-app-s-size) says the App Store limits how large an app can be when installed over a mobile connection, and that a person needs Wi-Fi once the app exceeds that limit. That page does not print the 200 MB number. The page that prints it is the build-metadata page: a yellow warning appears next to the build and next to the variant, and Apple emails you, when any variant’s download size exceeds the 200 MB over-the-air download limit.

This skill did not find a current `developer.apple.com` page that quotes the on-device prompt text. Do not invent the wording of that prompt. Do keep every thinned variant’s compressed download under 200 MB so a cellular install is not the case the warning describes. Well under 100 MB is the budget.

The final size is not the IPA you uploaded. After approval the binary is encrypted and recompressed, and it can grow. App Store Connect’s per-variant sizes, after processing, are the sizes to trust. The same build-metadata page says the exact final size cannot be known in advance.

### Thinning

App thinning is Apple building a smaller variant per device and OS. On the product page, iOS shows the install size for the device that is viewing the page. The universal variant is the one for older install paths (iOS 8 and earlier, volume purchase, older iTunes). Sources: [Maximum build file sizes](https://developer.apple.com/help/app-store-connect/reference/app-uploads/maximum-build-file-sizes/) and [View builds and metadata](https://developer.apple.com/help/app-store-connect/manage-builds/view-builds-and-metadata/).

Slicing is that per-device variant. Measure the variant a phone will actually download, not the universal IPA.

Bitcode is not a thinning tool you can still use. Starting with Xcode 14, Apple no longer accepts bitcode submissions. The build-metadata page says dSYM downloads for bitcode exist only for older submissions. Do not enable bitcode to shrink a new app.

### On-Demand Resources and Background Assets

On-Demand Resources are deprecated as of iOS 27, iPadOS 27, tvOS 27, and visionOS 27, and support will be removed in future releases. Starting in early 2027, App Store Connect will no longer accept uploads that contain On-Demand Resources from new apps or from apps that have never used the feature. Migrate to Background Assets. Source: [On-Demand Resources size limits](https://developer.apple.com/help/app-store-connect/reference/app-uploads/on-demand-resources-size-limits/).

Do not introduce On-Demand Resources in a new app. [Background Assets](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/backgroundassets) can download extra files before first launch, in the background, or on demand, and assets can update without a new app build. If you use Apple-hosted Background Assets, the product page shows an “Up to” size that includes non-localized essential packs and the largest single language of localized essential packs ([Maximum build file sizes](https://developer.apple.com/help/app-store-connect/reference/app-uploads/maximum-build-file-sizes/)).

For the price-tag scanner, do not put text recognition or the trip ledger in a download that can be absent at first launch. The core flow has to work in a store with no signal. See `offline-and-scanning.md`.

## Google Play

New apps have had to publish an Android App Bundle since August 2021. Source: [About Android App Bundles](https://developer.android.com/guide/app-bundle). The same banner appears on [APK Expansion Files](https://developer.android.com/google/play/expansion-files).

All Play size limits below are **compressed download size**, computed by Play Console on upload. `bundletool` is a close estimate, not the same number. Source: [Play app size limits](https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/9859372?hl=en).

| Component | Compressed download limit | Kind |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Base module | 500 MB | Store limit |
| Each feature module | 500 MB | Store limit |
| Each asset pack | 1.5 GB | Store limit |
| All modules plus install-time asset packs, together | 4 GB | Store limit |
| Asset packs delivered on demand or fast-follow, together | 30 GB | Store limit |
| Total of those caps | 34 GB | Store limit |

Play’s own note on that page: keep the app as small as possible, and most apps should stay well below these limits.

Above **200 MB**, a person installing on mobile data sees a non-blocking dialog that the app is large. That is a store warning, not a failed upload. Source: the same size-limits page.

### What 200 MB is, and what it is not

A request that says “about 200 MB initial download, unless you add expansion files” is describing an older shape of the rules. State the current numbers instead.

- The current hard cap on the base module is **500 MB** compressed, not 200 MB.
- The current cap on the install (modules plus install-time asset packs) is **4 GB** compressed.
- **200 MB** is the size at which Play shows a non-blocking mobile-data dialog.
- The app-bundle page and the expansion-files page both say that new apps larger than 200 MB are supported by Play Feature Delivery or Play Asset Delivery. That sentence records when those features became the way to ship a large app. It is not a current 200 MB hard cap.
- Apps that still publish APKs, instead of bundles, are on the legacy APK cap: **100 MB** compressed. That is a different, older path. Source: the size-limits page.

[About Android App Bundles](https://developer.android.com/guide/app-bundle) also says the compressed APKs required to install (base plus configuration splits) must be no more than 4 GB, and that any later on-demand feature-module download must meet that restriction too. It adds that asset packs do not contribute to that APK-set limit and have their own limits. The Play Console table is more specific: **install-time** asset packs count toward the 4 GB cumulative total. When you are deciding whether an upload will be rejected, use the Play Console table. Re-read both pages if they diverge further.

### Asset delivery, feature delivery, and OBB

[Play Asset Delivery](https://developer.android.com/guide/playcore/asset-delivery) is how a bundle carries large assets. It describes itself as the replacement for legacy expansion files (OBB) for games larger than 200 MB.

| Mode | When it arrives | Counts toward the size listed on Play | May be missing later |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Install-time | With the install, as split APKs | Yes | No. The person cannot delete these. |
| Fast-follow | Right after install, without opening the app | No | Yes. Play or the person may remove them. |
| On-demand | While the app is running | No | Yes. Same as fast-follow. |

Install-time packs also count toward the 4 GB cumulative limit in the table above. Fast-follow and on-demand packs use the separate 30 GB cap. Do not put anything the first screen needs into fast-follow or on-demand. The price-tag scanner’s recognizer belongs in the base module.

[Play Feature Delivery](https://developer.android.com/guide/playcore/feature-delivery) is the same idea for code modules. A module the first scan needs is not an on-demand module.

App bundles do not support APK expansion (`*.obb`) files. Source: [About Android App Bundles](https://developer.android.com/guide/app-bundle). The expansion-files guide still documents the old APK path (a compressed APK of at most 100 MB, plus up to two expansion files of 2 GB each) and then tells you to use a bundle, which allows up to a 500 MB compressed download, instead of expansion files. Treat OBB as legacy. Do not add it to a new app.

## Price-tag scanner

The scanner’s download should be the base install: app code, the on-device recognizer, and any small offline table (for example a tax-rate table). No expansion file, no On-Demand Resources, no fast-follow pack on the critical path. Hold the line at the budgets in `budgets.md`, which sit well under 100 MB and under the 200 MB warning on both stores.
